title: Integrated flood risk and transport-network resilience in Baghdad using an EHCR–TOPSIS framework
content:
by Hasanain Hikmat Khudhair, Zahra Azizi, Aminreza Neshat, Jalil Imani Harsini

This study presents an integrated geospatial framework for prioritizing flood risk across Baghdad’s urban road network. The framework combines four dimensions—Exposure (E), Hazard (H), Criticality (C), and Redundancy (R)—using the Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS). The indicators were derived from widely available datasets, including the SRTM DEM, Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2 imagery, CHIRPS precipitation, hydrographic data, and OpenStreetMap roads. At the road-segment level, they describe proximity to flood-prone hydrogeomorphic settings, terrain and hydroclimatic controls, network importance, and the availability of alternative routes. Several parameter scenarios were tested to account for plausible differences in rainfall concentration, drainage density, and proximity thresholds, and the resulting risk classes were independently compared with Sentinel-1 SAR-derived inundation observations from the 2019 and 2022 events. TOPSIS closeness coefficients ranged from 0.17 to 0.89. About 28% of the total road length was classified as High or Very High risk, mainly along eastern and northeastern corridors near the Tigris River and channelized lowlands. The pooled flood-capture rate was 80.35%, meaning that roughly four-fifths of the independently observed inundated road locations fell within the two highest EHCR–TOPSIS classes. These maps can support preparedness, emergency routing, and the prioritization of maintenance and retrofitting in data-scarce settings. The approach may also be adapted to other flood-prone cities with similar hydrogeomorphic and infrastructure constraints.
